prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map captures a large indoor warehouse with a high corrugated roof above, a flat floor below, tall stacks of white blocks about 4–8 metres to the left and 8–12 metres to the right, and distant walls with a dark doorway about 15–20 metres ahead. In the foreground within arm's reach (0.2–0.5 metres) is the back of another person's head wearing a head-mounted device (partially cropped at the bottom of frames 1–4 and absent in frame 5) and the camera wearer's own raised right hand and forearm in frame 2, which partially occlude the lower-left block stack and equipment behind them. Across frames 1 to 4, the camera wearer turns rightward and tilts upward—causing the left block stack and foreground head to shift left while a right-side block stack and a nearby rectangular box (about 2–3 metres away on the right) enter frame 4—before turning back to the left in frame 5 as the nearby person moves lower and out of view. The depth map makes the continuous ground-plane gradient and the distinct distance separation between the 0.3-metre foreground head/hand, the 4–6-metre left block stack, and the 15-metre background wall much clearer than in RGB alone. However, it is unreliable in frame 4 where the high ceiling above is rendered bright as if only 1–2 metres away, and across all frames it completely misses the distant people standing and crouching near a cart about 15–18 metres away by the far doorway.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates foreground and background regions across the warehouse floor, capturing thecamera wearer's right arm at 0.3 metres in frame 2, the nearby person's head at 0.3–0.5 metres in the lower foreground of frame 3 (facing away from the camera wearer toward the warehouse interior), and one of the distant standing workers about 15–18 metres ahead near the far wall. In the RGB context, two distant workers (one standing, one crouching within 1–2 metres of each other and within arm's reach of a small cart) are positioned in front of the windowed wall to the left of the large dark doorway, alongside a third person in red standing about 8–10 metres away near the right block stack in frame 4; none of these distant figures look toward the camera wearer. As the camera pans right from frame 1 to frame 4 and back left in frame 5, the segmented distant worker shifts from the left-center background to the far left of frame 4 and back to the center-right in frame 5, while the foreground head and raised arm appear and disappear at the bottom edge. While segmentation helps pinpoint the tiny distant standing worker against the cluttered background wall across frames 1–5, it is highly unreliable in classification and completeness. Specifically, it mislabels the foreground person's hair as a 'cat' in frames 1–2, mislabels the 4–6-metre left block stack as a 'keyboard' in frames 1–2, mislabels a partial piece of equipment ~2–3 metres to the lower-left as a 'bicycle' in frame 3, misses the foreground head in frame 4, and fails to segment the crouching worker near the cart or the person near the right stack.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map is almost entirely blank across the 5 frames, detecting only a single magenta 3D-projected hand skeleton for the camera wearer's own raised right hand in the lower-left foreground of frame 2. This hand is positioned about 0.3 metres in front of the camera wearer—well within arm's reach and immediately to the right of the nearby person's head (which is ~0.2 metres from the hand and facing away)—with fingers curled leftward toward the head-mounted camera strap on that person. Across frames 1, 3, 4, and 5, the camera wearer's hand is out of view below the frame, and the camera rotates rightward from the left block stack toward the right block stack before turning back left in frame 5. The pose map clearly reveals the exact joint articulation and finger curvature of the camera wearer's raised hand in frame 2 despite motion blur and skin-Against-background contrast in the RGB image. However, the map is unreliable for broader scene understanding because it detects no yellow body skeletons at all—completely missing the heavily occluded foreground person whose head and shoulders are at the bottom edge of frames 1–4, the two distant workers standing and crouching 1–2 metres apart near the cart at 15–18 metres, and the person standing ~8–10 metres away on the right in frame 4.
